subject: Cooking
title: Saffron: The World's Most Expensive Spice
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Saffron: The World's Most Expensive Spice.

hook.text: One pound of saffron costs up to $5,000. It takes 75,000 crocus flowers to produce that single pound.

buildup.text: Each crocus produces just three tiny red stigmas. They must be hand-picked during a two-week harvest.

discovery.text: Saffron's flavor comes from safranal, its color from crocin — both are powerful at microscopic doses.

twist.text: Saffron fraud is rampant — turmeric, safflower, and dyed corn silk are common counterfeits.

climax.text: Iran produces 90% of the world's saffron, with traditions dating back over 3,000 years.

punchline.text: The most expensive spice is three threads from a flower.

quiz.question: Which country produces about 90% of the world's saffron?

details.summary: Saffron costs up to $10,000 per kilogram because each crocus flower produces only three tiny stigmas, harvested by hand. It takes 150,000 flowers to make one kilogram. Saffron contributes golden color from crocin, bitter depth from picrocrocin, and a distinctive aroma from safranal.
details.whyItMatters: Saffron's extreme labor requirements and unique chemistry make it irreplaceable in dishes like paella, risotto Milanese, and Persian rice. No synthetic substitute replicates all three of its properties.
takeaways: 150,000 flowers yield just one kilogram of saffron threads
Crocin provides color, picrocrocin provides flavor, safranal aroma
Iran produces about 90 percent of the world's saffron supply

faq.question: How can you tell if saffron is real or fake?
faq.answer: Real saffron threads are trumpet-shaped with uneven color, darker at the tips. They release color slowly in warm water over minutes. Fakes like dyed corn silk release color instantly and often dissolve. Real saffron smells honey-sweet with metallic notes, not musty.

faq.question: Why is saffron so expensive?
faq.answer: Each crocus flower produces only three stigmas, hand-picked during a two-week harvest window. Workers harvest at dawn before flowers fully open. Drying must be precise. The entire process uses no machinery. This extreme labor intensity drives the price above gold per gram in some markets.
